paras: The Epes fire and expulsion of 1882 was a clash in Epes, Sumter County, Alabama, on June 3, 1882, in which white men drove a crowd of Black men out of town and the town was burned that night. Seven stores burned, four Black men accused of setting the fire were arrested at Tuscaloosa, and papers reported fears that they would be lynched. The story ran widely in the white press as a case of "negro incendiaries" and "negro rioters."

According to a dispatch from Tuscaloosa, a crowd of "drunken negroes" became "very boisterous in the streets" of Epes on Saturday afternoon, "insulting the citizens and threatening violence." The white men of the town "banded together and drove the turbulent crowd out of town," the dispatch said, without describing how. After nightfall the town was set on fire, and the dispatch charged the fire to the men who had been driven out. Seven stores burned and the town was described as "almost totally destroyed"; one news summary later put the loss at $25,000.

A second dispatch, dated at Chattanooga and elsewhere credited to Decatur, called the affair "a riot" between whites and blacks at "Epps Station" and said the Black men returned "at midnight." No deaths or injuries were reported on either side.

Four Black men "implicated in the burning" boarded the up train on the Alabama Great Southern Railroad and were arrested when it reached Tuscaloosa, where they were jailed to be returned to Epes. Others were reported pursued, and the second dispatch said "it is feared they will be lynched if captured." An Ohio digest added that "the respectable negroes" were incensed and "would not interfere if the whites took such a step." The coverage names none of the men and reports no lynching, trial or other outcome.

The Tuscaloosa dispatch reached papers from Maine to Utah on June 6 under headlines such as "A DRUNKEN MOB" and "NEGRO INCENDIARIES." Western and Midwestern weeklies reprinted it in fire and news columns over the next days, garbling the town's name as "Epis" and "Eyres." The Memphis Daily Appeal used the more neutral heading "Riot Between Whites and Blacks in Alabama," and that version circulated in Ohio and Mississippi papers through June 21. Shorter Southern items reduced the story to Epes being "set on fire by a crowd of rioting blacks."
Every account came from white sources and gave the white townspeople's version of why the men were driven out. No Black-press coverage of the episode was found.

The Tuscaloosa dispatch, filed on June 4 and 5, placed the fire on Saturday night, June 3, while the Chattanooga dispatch said "Monday night" and one Oregon reprint said "the 5th." The earlier dispatch from nearby Tuscaloosa is the better guide to the date.

reader.title: Epes fire and expulsion of 1882
bases: White men 'banded together and drove the turbulent crowd' of Black men out of Epes, the core act of white force reported (A2, A4, A6); the burning of the town that followed was charged to the Black men driven out, not to whites (A2, A6).

Two separately datelined dispatches, from Tuscaloosa (A2, A4) and from Chattanooga/Decatur (A6, A10), agree that whites drove Black men from Epes, that they returned and burned seven stores, and that arrests followed, though they differ on the day and both give only the white side.

accounts.label: Tuscaloosa wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Drunken Black men insulted citizens and threatened violence; white men drove them out; they came back after nightfall, fired the town, and four were arrested at Tuscaloosa.

accounts.label: Chattanooga/Decatur dispatch
accounts.gist: A 'riot' between whites and blacks at Epps Station ended with the Black men driven from town; they returned at midnight and burned seven stores; arrests and pursuit followed and lynching was feared.

framing.detail: The Tuscaloosa dispatch ran under 'A DRUNKEN MOB' and 'NEGRO INCENDIARIES' and presented the driving out as a response to 'turbulent' drunken Black men.
The Chattanooga version was headed 'Riot Between Whites and Blacks in Alabama' and named no provocation.
Northern and western papers carried the Tuscaloosa text in fire and news columns; Mississippi and Louisiana papers ran one-line items on 'rioting blacks' and 'Negro rioters'.

conflicts.note: The Tuscaloosa dispatch was filed June 4 and June 5 and is nearer the event; the Monday date in the later Chattanooga dispatch is likely an error.
